SA Assembly and SAB > SAB Format Whitepaper (Specification)

SAB Format Whitepaper

This page is the normative specification of the SAB binary format: byte layout, encoding rules, the producer and consumer landscape, and the round-trip and version contracts. For a format overview, see the SAB Bytecode Format Overview page; this page is the byte-level specification, and implementers can independently implement a SAB producer/consumer from this text alone.

Sources and pinned versionsEvery format fact in this text takes the source code as authoritative and cites its source (file:line). Pinned versions for line-number verification: sci 2e67cc54, sa_plugin_sla 0cc23855 (2026-11-05). Existing documents (sci/docs/design.md, sci/docs/sab_evaluation.md, sci/docs/sab_distributed_compilation.md) serve only as leads; where they conflict with the source code, the source code prevails, and the conflict list is in Appendix B.

0. Terminology

  • SA text: .sa human-readable assembly text, parsed/macro-expanded by the host Flattener into an instruction stream.
  • SAB: .sab, the binary serialization format of the SA instruction stream, and the specification object of this text.
  • Instruction: a flat three-address instruction (the Instruction struct in sci/src/common/instruction.zig), the convergence representation of the text path and the SAB path.
  • Referee: the host verifier (sci/src/verifier.zig / sci/src/referee/), which checks the instruction stream for ownership/capability/state consistency.
  • FlattenResult: the host-internal flat program representation (instructions + constant declarations + function signatures + symbol table + ancillary information such as positions/layout), constructed separately by the text path and the SAB path before converging.
  • Producer: a component that writes out .sab bytes; consumer: a component that reads in .sab bytes.

The specification object of this text is the wire format itself: an implementer can independently implement a producer/consumer from the byte layout in this text, without linking sci's implementation code. The “SLA plugin and host share the same encode/decode source code” described in §3 is a current engineering fact, not a format requirement.

1. Positioning and Design Motivation

Current position (user ruling, 2026-11-15) Production first: SLA's production path is SA text. All frontends (SLA, slars, the Rust implementation, and any third-party frontend) output only SA text. The Zig version of the SLA compiler's default backend has been changed to SA text, and SAB requires an explicit compiler flag (--test-backend sab, opt-in). SAB was sealed on 2026-11-15 (sealing tag sab-sealed-2026-11-15, placed on the then-current heads of the sci / sa_plugin_sla / sla repositories): SAB is an optimization direction, not a production threshold; the old positioning in this section, “SAB is the production-path interchange format, and SA text is retained only as a teaching and decompilation/debugging mirror”, is hereby abolished. If SAB is unsealed in the future, its only form will be a text → SAB one-way conversion inside the SA toolchain (the SA instruction set is closed and already frozen, so the converter needs to be written only once): frontends will never emit SAB, nor be aware of its existence; a reverse conversion (disassembling to recover text) is unnecessary — SAB is always derived from text, and text is always the source. Two measured positions were pinned in the same batch: first, SAB does not accelerate a single compilation (the bulk of cold-compilation time is in the host backend, unrelated to whether the input takes the text or SAB path); second, hot compilation / incremental caching is an independent mechanism keyed by source hash, unrelated to SAB. SAB's only concrete residual use is DLL-like customer delivery: giving the customer a .sab rather than the source, so the customer compiles it directly with the SA compiler to confirm (sa build accepts .sab input, and the text side produces it via --emit-sab) and verifies behavior, without obtaining the source; its protection strength is at the same level as a DLL (the instruction stream can be reverse-engineered and restored, while the original text / naming / comments are not attached), and it must not be described as source-level confidentiality. The honesty rule is unchanged: a missing lowering in any backend must report loudly, with silent fallback forbidden — that is a ban on false greens, not a route priority. The remaining chapters of this whitepaper are the specification of the format itself (byte layout, encoding and round-trip contracts), and do not lapse because of the sealing; the producer / consumer landscape in §3 describes the implementation state at the sealing point in time.

The following four points are the original design motivations (historical) when SAB was introduced, retained for reference; their current assessment is governed by the position at the start of this section (motivation 1's throughput claim was never independently measured and delivered, motivation 2's frontend/backend binary handover has exited with the production-path change, and motivation 3's caching and distributed work has not landed, with caching now characterized as an independent mechanism unrelated to SAB):

  1. Compilation throughput: SAB decoding goes directly to structured Instruction[], skipping the volume amplification of text parsing, macro expansion, and @import expansion (the Y-shaped dual-input architecture in §3 of sci/docs/design.md; that document claims the binary path's steady-state time is about 1/10 of the text path — this is the design document's figure, and this whitepaper has not independently benchmark-verified it, see §6).
  2. A unified interchange format for the plugin architecture: SA is the common target of multiple frontends (SLA, slars, and future RS/TS frontends). Frontends and the host hand over via a binary instruction package whose layout is fixed, versioned, and source-language-independent, rather than having the host re-parse each frontend's text output.
  3. The foundation for incremental / caching / distributed work: a module carries its own symbols + signatures + constants + instructions in four parts (see §2), providing a format foundation for function-level caching, content hashes, and module-level parallelism (the related capabilities are under construction; external references such as extern functions and native-text targets are still resolved against the host context, so a module is not fully self-contained). Distributed compilation among them is currently still a design draft (sci/docs/sab_distributed_compilation.md status: design draft), not landed (see §6).
  4. Human/machine division of labor: text for humans (readable, teachable, debuggable), binary for machines (compact, verifiable, cacheable).

2. Format Overview

Primary source: sci/src/sab.zig (referred to below as sab.zig, with all line numbers referring to that file); the definition source for instructions and operands: sci/src/common/instruction.zig (referred to as instruction.zig); signatures and types: sci/src/common/signature.zig (referred to as signature.zig); constant declarations: sci/src/common/const_decl.zig (referred to as const_decl.zig).

2.1 File Layout

OffsetFieldEncodingSource
0magic4-byte fixed length "SAB\0" (0x53 0x41 0x42 0x00)sab.zig:10
4version_majoru8 fixed length, currently = 4sab.zig:11
5version_minoru8 fixed length, currently = 0 (semantics reserved, see §4.3)sab.zig:12
6section_countULEB128, the encoder always writes 4sab.zig:989-996
7…sections × section_countSee belowsab.zig:128-132

Offset 7 is the output when the current encoder writes section_count in its 1-byte shortest form; the decoder reads the count as ULEB128 and does not check for the shortest form, so this offset is not a format constant, and the general form is 6 + the ULEB byte length of section_count.

The wire format of each section: id: ULEB128 + payload_len: ULEB128 + payload (writeSection, sab.zig:128-132). Section id definitions (sab.zig:14-19):

idNameContents
1symbol_poolString pool (§2.3)
2function_sigsFunction signature table (§2.4)
3const_declsConstant declaration table (§2.5)
4instructionsInstruction stream (§2.6)

Producers must write all four sections in the order 1→2→3→4 (a specification requirement; the current encoder encodeProgramWithConsts does exactly this, sab.zig:993-996). Consumers are currently lenient about order, but out-of-order input triggers the pool-resolution dependency of §4.4, and producers must not exploit that leniency. The file has no trailing checksum, signature, or total-length ledger field (the complete write path in sab.zig:989-997 is the full picture of the file); decode errors and Referee verification can only reject structurally/semantically illegal content, and do not provide a guarantee of “detecting arbitrary content changes” (corruption that substitutes values within the legal value range may pass all checks, see §6.4).

2.2 Encoding Primitives

PrimitiveRuleSource
ULEB128Unsigned little-endian LEB128: the low 7 bits of each byte are payload, the high bit is the continuation bit. Decoding reads at most 10 bytes: for the 10th byte (shift 63) only the lowest payload bit enters the result and the remaining bits are shifted out of the u64 width and discarded; Leb128Overflow is reported only when the 10th byte still carries a continuation bitsab.zig:75-96
SLEB128Signed LEB128, at most 10 bytes; bit 6 of the terminating byte is the sign bit, and decoding performs sign extension when the total shift is <64sab.zig:98-126
Shortest formProducers must emit shortest-form LEB encodings (the current encoder is always shortest-form); the decoder accepts non-shortest forms without erroring on that accountsab.zig:75-126
Fixed-length bytesEnum-class fields (instruction kind, various enums) are written as their raw u8 enum ordinalSuch as writeInstructions starting at sab.zig:452
Optional fieldsPresence byte: 0 = absent, 1 = present followed by payload; any other presence value reports InvalidTagwriteOptionalEnum/readOptionalEnum etc. in sab.zig
Floating-point immediatesimm_float is written as the IEEE-754 bit pattern of an f64, as a fixed-length 8-byte little-endian u64, preserved bit-for-bit (including NaN payloads and -0.0); encoding/decoding performs no normalizationThe .imm_float branch in writeOperand starting at sab.zig:189
Pool indicesReferences to the string pool are written as ULEB128 pool indices; the encoder internally allocates pool ids as u32 (std.StringHashMap(u32)), and an out-of-range index reports InvalidTag at decode timesab.zig:189, starting at sab.zig:357

2.3 Section 1: symbol_pool (String Pool)

Wire format: count: ULEB128, followed by, for each entry, len: ULEB128 + len bytes of raw byte string (no NUL terminator) (writeStringPool, sab.zig:134-141).

The pool is the whole file's unified string interning table (i.e. the module's symbol table), carrying: symbol names, register names, function/parameter names, the text of .text / .native_text operands, file names (the file of upstream_loc), package identity, and all other text (for the pool's collection scope, see the pool-construction segment of encodeProgramWithConsts, sab.zig:935-988). Pool rules:

  • The encoder deduplicates by byte content (the same byte sequence is interned only once, same source as above); the decoder does not require the pool to be duplicate-free, and the index of a duplicate entry refers to its own entry.
  • Strings in the pool are arbitrary byte sequences, not required to be UTF-8, and the decoder performs no encoding validation.

Numbering namespaces (implementers must distinguish, item by item, where the ULEB128 payload of each operand/field points): .symbol and .reg are pool indices — the index of a .reg holds the corresponding register name, and the host resolves it via the pool when synthesizing text (operandRegName, see readOperand starting at sab.zig:357 and synthesizeRawText); .label / .func / .ty are, at the sab.zig layer, only numeric ids (disassembly presents them as L / fn: / ty: respectively, without pool resolution), and their correspondence to names is defined by the producer's symbol table / type table construction. A function signature's param_ids / reg_ids share the same symbol-table id space as .reg, and reg_ids is the set of register ids involved in that function (written from post-verification metadata, see the host bridge in §3.1).

The encoder is a deterministic function of its four groups of ordered inputs (the symbol sequence, constant declarations, function signatures, and the instruction stream): the pool is built in a fixed order — first the symbol order given by the caller, then text carried by instructions collected in instruction order, then function signatures, then constant declarations (sab.zig:935-988); the hash table is used only for lookup and does not participate in output ordering. Therefore identical inputs produce identical bytes (deterministic encoding). This is a different matter from “the same source program must produce the same bytes”: the latter also depends on whether the ordered inputs produced by the frontend are stable, which is outside this text's guarantee scope. Byte consistency across independent builds has been observed on measured samples (the .sab hashes of multiple builds of the same source file agree), with the evidence scope limited to the samples tested.

2.4 Section 2: function_sigs (Function Signature Table)

Wire format: count: ULEB128, followed by each signature written in a fixed field order (writeFunctionSigs, starting at sab.zig:642):

FieldEncodingNotes
idULEB128Function id
namePool index (ULEB128)
kindu8FunctionKind ordinal, 6 values in total: normal / ffi_wrapper / external / exported / test_func / gpu (signature.zig:92-101)
return_capOptional: presence + u8CapPrefix (see §2.6)
return_tyu8PrimType ordinal, 15 values in total (signature.zig:11-27)
return_fallibleu8 boolean
entry_inst_idxULEB128The function's entry index in the instruction stream
is_ffi_wrapper / ignored / should_panic / is_variadicEach a u8 boolean
upstream_fileOptional pool textv3+ metadata (see §4.3)
upstream_locOptional: pool-index file + ULEB128 line + ULEB128 colv3+ metadata
llvm_nameOptional pool textv3+ metadata
paramscount: ULEB128 + per parameter (name pool index, ty u8, cap u8)
param_idscount: ULEB128 + ULEB128 × n
reg_idscount: ULEB128 + ULEB128 × n

2.5 Section 3: const_decls (Constant Declaration Table)

Wire format: count: ULEB128, followed by each declaration (writeConstDecls, starting at sab.zig:595):

FieldEncodingNotes
source_line / expanded_lineEach ULEB128Source line / macro-expanded line
namePool index
literal_textPool indexThe literal's original text. It is format content, not optional metadata, and producers must write it; the decoder rebuilds the raw_text of @const name = literal_text from it (readConstDecls starting at sab.zig:607)
upstream_locOptional (same as §2.4)v3+ metadata
valueTag u8 + payload (recursive)ConstValue, see below

The tag of a ConstValue is the ordinal of ConstLiteralKind, 5 values in total (const_decl.zig:4-10), with payload rules (writeConstValue, starting at sab.zig:530):

TagPayload
hex / utf8 / repeatBytesLiteral: len: ULEB128 + raw bytes + repeat presence byte; if repeat is present, followed by repeat_count: ULEB128 + repeat_byte: u8 (starting at sab.zig:500)
struct_field_count: ULEB128 + per field (name pool index, size: ULEB128, value recursive)
vtableslot_count: ULEB128 + per slot (name pool index, func_name pool index)

2.6 Section 4: instructions (Instruction Stream)

This section describes the wire format of the current version (v4); the field differences of historical versions (v1–v3) are in the version matrix in §4.3. Wire format: count: ULEB128, followed by each instruction written in a fixed field order (writeInstructions, starting at sab.zig:452):

FieldEncodingNotes
kindu8InstKind ordinal, 40 values in total (instruction.zig:264-308, full table in Appendix A)
source_lineULEB128
expanded_lineULEB128The decoder preserves it as-is; overwriting it with the instruction ordinal is forbidden (a source comment inside readInstructions starting at sab.zig:880 explicitly states this discipline)
op_kindOptional: presence + u8OpKind ordinal, 56 values in total (instruction.zig:13-85, full table in Appendix A)
operandsAlways 4 operands, each encoded per the operand encoding (table below)Instruction.operands is a fixed-length [4]Operand (instruction.zig:318); unused slots are filled with .none (tag 0)
atomic_value_tyPresence byte + ULEB128The element-type ordinal of the atomic operation (value range is the PrimType ordinals)
atomic_ordering / atomic_second_ordering / atomic_rmw_opEach an optional enum (presence + u8)
atomic_expected_text / atomic_new_textEach optional pool textThe metadata region introduced in v3 (from this row to the upstream_loc row): in the v4 wire format it is always at this position, with the fields themselves presence-encoded and possibly empty; in the v1/v2 wire formats the whole segment does not exist
native_reg_namescount: ULEB128 + pool index × nSame as above (v3 onwards)
package_identityOptional pool textSame as above (v3 onwards)
package_source_sha256Presence byte + 32-byte fixed lengthSame as above (v3 onwards). Note: this is per-instruction source-provenance metadata, not a file integrity checksum
upstream_locOptional (same as §2.4)Same as above (v3 onwards)

Operand encoding: a 1-byte tag + tag-dependent payload (writeOperand/readOperand, starting at sab.zig:189 / sab.zig:357). 15 kinds in total (instruction.zig:246-262):

TagKindPayload
0noneNone
1regULEB128 (pool index, resolved to a register name, see §2.3)
2symbolULEB128
3labelULEB128
4funcULEB128
5imm_i64SLEB128
6imm_u64ULEB128
7imm_intSLEB128
8imm_float8-byte little-endian f64 bit pattern
9op_codeu8 (OpCode ordinal, 23 values in total, instruction.zig:178-237)
10cap_prefixu8 (CapPrefix: by_value=0 / borrow=1 / move=2 / raw=3, instruction.zig:6-11)
11offsetULEB128
12tyULEB128
13textPool index
14native_textPool index

Append-only discipline for enums: enums whose ordinals are carried as raw bytes, such as InstKind and FunctionKind, may only have new members appended at the end, and existing ordinals must not move — this is explicitly stated in source comments (instruction.zig:301-307: “SAB encodes the kind as a raw byte, so existing values must not move”; likewise signature.zig:98-100). This discipline is currently maintained by source comments and review; no static assertion on enum counts was found in the source (verified 2026-11-05), and it is a known fragility in format evolution.

Scope boundary: the semantics of each operand slot of each instruction kind (which slots are required, which slots must be .none, and the type requirements) are defined by SA instruction semantics and are outside this text's encoding-specification scope; this text specifies only their encoding container (always 4 slots, with unused slots filled with .none).

2.7 Decoder Overview

The host decode entry point is decodeModule (starting at sab.zig:1008): it checks the magic → reads major/minor → reads sections one by one according to section_count and dispatches by id. The decoder also provides two partial-decode entry points: decodeFunctionSigsOnly (sab.zig:1043, signatures only) and decodeTestFunctionSigsOnly (sab.zig:1076, retains only test_func signatures and skips their parameter details — lossy, only for fast collection of the test list, see §6). disasmModule (sab.zig:1106) renders a module as human-readable debug text; on proven samples, that text is rejected by the SA text parser with ForbiddenSyntax, so disasm does not constitute a normative round-trip path (see §4.1) and serves only as debug presentation.

The table above lists entry-point existence (per the dispatch code in cli.zig); the degree of end-to-end verification of SAB input varies by backend, and the known gaps on the execution surface are in §4.1 — this table must not be read as a per-backend verified checklist.

4. Contracts

This section writes specification requirements separately from implementation status: the specification is the format's promise to producers/consumers; status gaps are marked truthfully — gaps are not written into the specification, nor is the specification used to conceal gaps. The two kinds of items in this section must also be distinguished: wire-format contracts (§4.1's equivalence requirements, §4.4's decode behavior) and project governance decisions (the no-downgrade rule in §4.2, and the commitments marked as “policy decisions” in §4.3) — the latter are project decisions, not facts derivable from the current implementation, and should be read separately.

4.1 Round-Trip Symmetry (specification-level requirement)

SAB's round-trip requirements are divided into two levels, which must not be conflated:

  • L1 encode/decode round-trip: decode(encode(module)) is equivalent to the original module item by item in structured semantics (instruction kinds/operands/ signatures/constants/metadata). The equivalence domain requires three qualifications: first, it does not include per-instruction source text — v4 encoding does not carry Instruction.raw_text (a design decision, see §4.3), and the decoded per-instruction raw_text is always the empty string; constant declarations' literal_text is not in this category — it is format content (see §2.5). Second, when decoding v2/v3 files, the on-disk raw_text is read in first, and the text of the four kinds call / call_indirect / panic / panic_msg is synthesized by the decoder from structure only when what was read is empty (synthesizeRawText, starting at sab.zig:389; the fill-in condition is the raw_text.len == 0 check in readInstructions). Third, encode(decode(bytes)) does not promise byte identity: the decoder's normalization behaviors (discarding unknown sections, later duplicate sections overwriting earlier ones, ignoring trailing bytes, re-encoding old-version input as v4, see §4.4) all change the bytes; L1 equivalence is only about the module structure obtained by decoding.
  • L2 host-representation round-trip (specification goal, to be achieved): the same program via the SAB path and the text path should obtain equivalent verification conclusions and executable semantics; after the host decodes a .sab into a FlattenResult, re-encoding that representation (via encodeSabFromFlat) must be able to pass its own built-in verification, without trapping.

Status (L1): the built-in roundtrip tests in sab.zig cover per-InstKind and per-OpKind (sab.zig:1392), per- Operand (sab.zig:1427), v4 metadata combinations (sab.zig:1352), function signatures (sab.zig:1506), etc. Here “coverage” refers to the existence and coverage area of the tests; this whitepaper did not re-run that suite on the pinned version, and does not assert on that basis that L1 has been verified as passing on the current version.

Status (L2, evidence in four layers):

  1. Observed representation differences: in the FlattenResult constructed by loadSabFlat, loc_table is entirely null, layout_versions is empty, def_dict is empty, cached_macro_defs is empty, and package_identities is an empty table (sci/src/cli.zig:4706-4722), asymmetric with the text path's full-information representation.
  2. Reproduced failures: the host's re-encoding of its own decode product traps at verification (sa check x.sab --emit-sab out rc=1); a set of core samples (7 files / minimal reproductions) signal 11 or hang on the SAB path and pass on the text path.
  3. Layer determined: the defect segment is on the execution surface “after the plugin produces the .sab, after host verification”, and is unrelated to the verifier.
  4. Root cause undetermined: that whole-struct temporaries are materialized as a single register and mishandled at control-flow merge points is a standing hypothesis that has not been falsified by any probe; the three sub-surfaces within the segment (plugin encoding semantics / host decode fidelity / host emission) have not yet been cleanly separated. There are also about 89 @test cases with the same signature candidates (kinship census groups A–H, of which B–H, about 60, have not been touched by any fix line), whose attribution awaits later determination.

This gap has been layered, and fixing is in progress. Before the fix lands: L2's status is the specification goal is established, the implementation has not reached it; producers and tools must not rely on L2 (for example, must not assume the host can successfully re-encode a decode product).

4.2 No SAB Downgrade to Text

When the target is SAB, the only legal result of a missing lowering/registration or a decode failure is a loud error; silently rerouting a function or module through the text backend is forbidden (project governance decision, 2026-11-03). Source anchors: CLI source comments explicitly state “SAB encode path is standalone: it never falls back to .sa text” and “a corrupt .sab must fail loudly, never silently” (sci/src/cli.zig:8728, and the test check --emit-sab roundtrips through compileSource without text fallback starting at :10842); the corresponding producer-side item is UnsupportedSabDirectFeature (§3.1).

4.3 Version Compatibility Policy

Current behavior (per the decoder source):

  • The current version is 4.0 (sab.zig:11-12); the current encoder produces only v4, and v1–v3 are read-only, never written.
  • The decoder accepts major ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, and reports UnsupportedSabVersion for any other major (decodeModule, starting at sab.zig:1008). The minor byte is read but does not participate in the decision — any minor value is accepted. Note this is only the current read behavior: the semantics of minor are reserved for definition by future versions, and current producers always write 0; it does not constitute any compatibility-negotiation mechanism, and consumers must not assume any meaning for minor changes beyond safe ignorability.
  • Version capability matrix (defined by the decoder's conditional-read logic — old-version layouts have no independent document, and the decoder is the surviving definition of the old-version formats):
majorraw_text (per-instruction source text)full metadata (atomic text/native register names/package identity and hash/upstream location; upstream metadata of signatures and constants)
1NoNo
2Yes (presence + pool index, located after the operands)No
3YesYes
4No (removed in v4; structured semantics prevail)Yes

Conditional-read sources: has_raw_text = major >= 2 and major < 4 , has_full_metadata = major >= 3, synthesize_debug_text = major < 4 (decodeModule starting at sab.zig:1008).

Policy decisions (project governance decisions, not facts derived from the implementation):

  • Ordinal enums are append-only (§2.6). But note: appending only guarantees that existing ordinals do not move; it does not guarantee that old consumers can handle new values — old decoders loudly reject unknown enum bytes with InvalidTag (readOperand / the std.enums.fromInt … orelse InvalidTag in readInstructions); there is no silent misinterpretation, but there is currently no capability-negotiation mechanism either; adding an enum member is still a breaking change for old consumers and must be assessed together with the version policy.
  • Breaking changes must bump major; the decoder's read paths for old majors are retained (currently accepting 1–4; the retention period is determined by later version policy).

4.4 Decoder Robustness Boundaries (status)

There are 7 decode errors in total (sab.zig:21-29): InvalidSabMagic, UnsupportedSabVersion, MissingInstructionSection, TruncatedSab, Leb128Overflow, InvalidTag, OutOfMemory. The decoder performs only structural validation; semantic legality (ownership, state consistency) is borne by the Referee that follows. The current handling of malformed input (recorded truthfully, not a specification promise; the behavior sources in this paragraph are all decodeModule, starting at sab.zig:1008, except where otherwise noted):

  • Failure atomicity: on decode failure no partial module is returned — already-allocated content is cleaned up via errdefer and returned as an error, so the caller cannot obtain a half-finished Module.
  • Section handling: decoding processes sections one by one in file order and resolves references immediately against the symbol pool at that moment. Unknown section ids are skipped (the dispatch if-chain simply does not match and ignores their payload); order is not enforced, but if symbol_pool does not appear first, pool references in the other sections will be resolved against an empty pool and mostly fail with InvalidTag. For duplicate sections, the later decoder overwrites the earlier one (the result variable is reassigned), but the earlier-decoded section has already materialized strings against the old pool while the later decoder resolves against the new pool, so reference resolution within the same module may be inconsistent when the pool is declared twice — producers must not emit duplicate sections. Unconsumed tail bytes inside each section's payload are not validated (each read function returns after reading its counted items). After reading section_count sections, decoding returns, and bytes after that are not scanned.
  • Required and defaulted: only the instructions section is required; its absence reports MissingInstructionSection; when the other sections are absent the decoder treats them as empty tables, and section_count may be less than 4. Producers always write all four sections (§2.1).
  • Counts and narrowing: several count fields (pool entry count, instruction count, field count, etc.) allocate memory according to the decoded value first, with no independent “count cap” validation; a malformed huge value may cause a huge allocation and fail with OutOfMemory. Several u32 fields (the .reg / .symbol / .label / .func / .offset / .ty operands, signature id / entry_inst_idx, etc.) are narrowed with @intCast, and a value exceeding the u32 limit triggers a runtime panic rather than a format error (starting at sab.zig:357, starting at :681). Hence the seven explicit errors are not the entirety of malformed-input failure modes.
  • Field-level strictness varies: the presence byte of an optional field is strictly validated as 0/1 (readOptionalEnum etc.), while several boolean fields in signatures are read leniently as “byte == 1 is true, anything else is false” (such as return_fallible in readFunctionSigs, starting at sab.zig:681).

5. Positioning Among Peer Formats

SAB belongs, together with LLVM bitcode, the WebAssembly binary format, and SPIR-V, to the format family of “binary IR + text mirror + load-time verification”: the text form is for humans to read, write, and debug, and the binary form is for efficient machine handover; the ecosystems of these formats generally treat round-trip fidelity as a specification topic; on top of this, SAB establishes its own two-level L1/L2 requirements (§4.1), without relying on analogy. Differences from family members: first, SAB's verification is not limited to type/structure legality, but also includes the host Referee's ownership and state semantic checks; second, SAB is simultaneously an in-process interchange format (the frontend plugin and the host share the same encode/decode implementation, see §3.1) and a file interchange format, rather than serving only for distribution or archiving. (2026-11-15 position update: the in-process interchange role has exited with the SAB sealing — frontends and the host now hand over via SA text; what remains of SAB is only the file format itself, and its residual role inside the SA toolchain, derived one-way from text, as a distribution / precompilation format, see §1.)

6. Known Limitations and Unimplemented Items (observation basis marked per item)

  1. No incremental append encoding: the encoding API has only three whole-module write-out entry points (encodeProgramWithConsts / encodeProgram / encodeModule, sab.zig:935-1007); after a module is modified it must be re-serialized as a whole module; this is an encoding-layer granularity and does not concern the granularity of compilation/lowering/caching. Function-level incrementality and module-level distributed compilation remain at the design-draft stage (sci/docs/sab_distributed_compilation.md).
  2. Package distribution does not use .sab: within sci/src/pkg/, no .sab distribution path was found (a grep on 2026-11-05 found no hits); whether package distribution in other components supports .sab is outside this round's verification scope. The known status is that packages are distributed as text .sa (per sab_evaluation.md, which calls this a design decision, but the rationale is not written in the source).
  3. Decode performance unmeasured: decoding is cursor-based, byte-by-byte LEB reading (the Cursor in sab.zig:52-73 and decodeUleb128 starting at sab.zig:86), with no bulk/ vectorized path; this text attaches no decode performance figures, and design.md's “about 1/10” is a design figure only (see §1).
  4. No file-level integrity mechanism: no checksum/signature (§2.1); decoding and the Referee can only reject structurally/semantically illegal content, and corruption that substitutes values within the legal value range may pass all checks, with no a-priori integrity rejection layer.
  5. Partial decoding is lossy: decodeTestFunctionSigsOnly retains only test_func signatures and discards parameter and id details (starting at sab.zig:1076); it is a dedicated fast path for test tooling, and no complete consumer may misuse it.
  6. L2 round-trip gap: see §4.1 (fix in progress).
  7. Consistency test materials are still incomplete: Appendix C gives the empty-module golden vector, which has actually been run for encode/decode verification on the pinned sci (2026-11-05); golden vectors with function signatures/metadata and a cross-implementation consistency suite are still missing. Note: when producers and consumers share the same encode/decode implementation, a shared error on both sides cannot be discovered by round-trip tests, so cross-checking with an independent implementation is therefore necessary.

Appendix C: Empty-Module Golden Vector (run-verified)

All bytes written by encodeModule for a module with zero symbols, zero signatures, zero constants, and zero instructions (19 bytes). This vector was actually run and verified on 2026-11-05 on the pinned sci 2e67cc54 source tree with Zig 0.17.0: calling sab.encodeModule (empty symbols, empty instructions) produced the bytes below; reading them back with sab.decodeModule gave counts of 0 in all four sections; encoding the decode result again with encodeModule produced bytes identical byte-for-byte to the first output.
